9.  Approve Property Tax Rates for Fiscal Year 2026-27 (Districts: All)

  Overview
  This is a request to set the annual countywide ad valorem tax rates and the tax rates for school
  district debt service funds.

  State law requires that these rates be adopted by the Board of Supervisors (Board) on or before
  October 3rd annually so the rates can be used to prepare the property tax roll and property tax
  bills. State law also requires that taxes be levied upon the taxable property of the County.

  Recommendation by Chief Administrative Officer:
  Adopt the resolution entitled: “A RESOLUTION OF THE BOARD OF SUPERVISORS OF
  THE COUNTY OF SAN DIEGO ADOPTING THE PROPERTY TAX RATES FOR THE
  FISCAL YEAR COMMENCING JULY 1, 2026” (Attachment A, on file with the Clerk of the
  Board) incorporating the various rates as computed by the Auditor and Controller for Fiscal Year
  2026-27.

  Equity Impact Statement
  General Obligation Bonds are a vital financing mechanism for school districts in our community.
  The proceeds from the voter approved bonds are used to provide much needed infrastructure and
  equipment to school districts that might not otherwise have the resources for the acquisition
  and/or construction of these public improvements. There is strong evidence that high-quality
  infrastructure facilitates better instruction, improves student outcomes, and reduces dropout
  rates, among other benefits. School districts must conduct an annual, independent performance
  and financial audit.

  Sustainability Impact Statement
  The proposed action supports the County of San Diego Strategic Initiative of Sustainability.
  Supporting school districts by authorizing the Fiscal Year 2026-27 property tax rates will raise
  the funds necessary to make the annual principal and interest payments on voter approved
  bonded debt.

  Fiscal Impact
  There is no fiscal impact associated with the adoption of this resolution. There will be no change
  in net General Fund cost and no additional staff years.

16.  Receive Presentation on the Draft Economic Impact Study and Recommendations on the
  Tijuana River Sewage Crisis (Districts: All)

  Recommendation by Chief Administrative Officer:
  Receive a presentation with the draft preliminary findings of the Economic Costs and Impacts of
  the Tijuana River Sewage Crisis study in response to the Board’s September 9, 2025 (17),
  direction.

Tuesday, September 15, 2026  9
   1)  ..End

  Equity Impact Statement
  The communities most directly affected by the Tijuana River sewage crisis include areas with
  socioeconomic and demographic characteristics that may increase vulnerability to economic and
  environmental disruptions. The draft study identifies a primary study area with approximately
  155,265 residents and 47,759 households. The study reports higher unemployment, a higher
  share of renters and cost-burdened renter households, lower educational attainment, and a higher
  share of households with incomes below $75,000 compared with the overall region. Presenting
  the draft findings supports a more complete understanding of how the crisis affects communities
  that have experienced prolonged exposure to pollution and related economic disruption.

  Sustainability Impact Statement
  Presentation of the draft findings supports the County of San Diego’s efforts to understand and
  address the long-term environmental, economic, and community impacts of the Tijuana River
  sewage crisis. The study provides information that can help guide investments and policy actions
  intended to improve environmental conditions, community well-being, economic resilience, and
  the long-term sustainability of affected communities.

  Fiscal Impact
  There is no fiscal impact associated with today’s presentation on the economic impacts of the
  Tijuana River sewage crisis. There will be no change in General Fund cost and no additional
  staff years.

  Business Impact Statement
  The draft study identifies significant pathways through which the sewage crisis has and may
  continue to affect businesses, including reduced beach visitation and tourism, lower customer
  activity, business disinvestment, and changes in business starts. Business survey respondents
  reported revenue impacts and indicated that continued conditions could result in reduced
  staffing, lost income, closure, or relocation. Draft recommendations include expanding
  economic-development and technical assistance for affected businesses, promoting destinations
  and activities that remain available during beach water closures, supporting events that increase
  foot traffic, connecting businesses with financial and marketing resources, and promoting South
  Bay assets and investment opportunities.

  Advisory Board Statement
  N/A

  Background
  The Tijuana River sewage crisis has affected communities and coastal areas in the South Bay for
  decades. Sewage and other pollutants carried through the Tijuana River watershed have
  contributed to prolonged beach water closures, degraded water and air quality, public health
  concerns, reduced recreational access, and economic disruption in affected communities.

  On September 9, 2025 (17), the San Diego County Board of Supervisors (Board) approved an
  item entitled, “Enhancing Regional Efforts and Federal Advocacy to Advance Solutions to the
  Tijuana River Sewage Crisis.” As part of that action, the Board directed the Chief
  Administrative Officer to fund and implement an Economic Impact Study assessing the full

Tuesday, September 15, 2026  10
   scope of losses caused by the sewage crisis, including impacts to small businesses, property
  values, and regional tourism, to strengthen future funding and mitigation efforts.

  The resulting Economic Costs and Impacts of the Tijuana River Sewage Crisis study is designed
  to identify and measure economic costs and impacts associated with the crisis and to provide
  evidence supporting a proactive approach to addressing those impacts. The draft methodology
  acknowledges that certain impacts can be monetized and directly attributed to the sewage crisis.
  It further recognizes that additional impacts can be quantified, though not reliably converted into
  monetary terms or conclusively linked to the crisis. Still others can be described or identified but
  cannot be appropriately quantified with the information currently available.

  The draft analysis identifies a series of negative economic impacts, including worsening water
  and air quality and prolonged beach water closures caused by increased sewage flows. These
  conditions have, in turn, contributed to reduced tourism and recreation, lost recreation value,
  costs to local businesses, property value declines, decreased transient occupancy tax revenues,
  increased public health and water treatment costs, population outmigration, and potential
  reductions in public school funding. The findings also identify potential impacts to public
  schools, with impacted districts experiencing larger reductions in enrollment and average daily
  attendance than other school districts in the region. Government expenditures associated with
  addressing the crisis are another component of the preliminary analysis. The study identifies
  approximately $1.3 billion in government spending to date based on various government reports,
  documents, websites, and news sources.

  Preliminary analysis indicates that the sewage crisis is causing substantial regional economic
  losses, with annual reductions in San Diego County’s economic output estimated between
  $125.6 million and $503.5 million and discounted cumulative 20-year impacts ranging from $1.9
  billion to $7.9 billion (in 2025 dollars). These estimates should be viewed as indicating the
  potential scale of economic effects, not as final damage determinations.

  Community and stakeholder engagement conducted for the study further illustrates these impacts
  on residents and businesses. This engagement took multiple forms, including virtual meetings
  with stakeholder discussion groups. These sessions gathered qualitative data such as anecdotes,
  stories, and lived experience. Invited stakeholders included municipal officials, environmental
  regulators, business leaders, chamber of commerce representatives, health experts, and
  community leaders. Additional community input was gathered via an online portal with four
  targeted surveys that were heavily promoted through multiple channels. Participants in the
  discussion groups and survey respondents reported reduced recreational activity, shorter or less
  frequent visits to impacted areas, concerns about health and quality-of-life, losses in business
  revenue, decreased staffing needs, and the potential for business closure or relocation if current
  conditions persist.

  The draft recommendations include providing consistent real-time communication to the
  affected communities across agencies and jurisdictions, providing support for affected
  businesses through promotional and technical assistance activities, strengthening regional and
  binational coordination, and advocating for long-term infrastructure reliability. The findings also
  recommend support for the San Diego Regional Chamber of Commerce’s 5-Pillar Framework,
  predictable funding for operations and maintenance, preventive maintenance and monitoring,

   and a coordinated binational approach that moves the region from reactive repairs toward
  proactive system management.

  The findings and recommendations presented today remain preliminary until the final report by
  ECOnorthwest is delivered in October 2026. Additional analysis and refinement are underway,
  including further evaluation of recreation and tourism losses, air-quality-related public health
  costs, property assessed values, and public-school funding implications. By receiving an update
  on the draft findings, the Board will have an opportunity to review the study’s current analysis
  and recommendations while the work is finalized. Receipt of today’s presentation on the draft
  preliminary findings does not constitute adoption of the findings or recommendations and does
  not authorize implementation of future actions requiring separate Board approval. The final
  report may include recommendations that, subject to the Board’s future consideration and
  direction, may require funding.

  Linkage To The County Of San Diego Strategic Plan
  Today’s action to receive the draft preliminary findings of the Economic Costs and Impacts of
  the Tijuana River Sewage Crisis study supports the “Equity” and “Community” Strategic
  Initiatives in the County of San Diego’s 2026-2031 Strategic Plan by providing data and analysis
  that can inform efforts to improve community quality of life, advance environmental justice,
  strengthen economic resilience, and protect the health and well-being of residents and businesses
  affected by the Tijuana River sewage crisis.

  Respectfully submitted,

18.  Strengthening Wage Theft Enforcement to Recover Stolen Wages and Protect Working
  Families (Districts: All)

  Recommendation by Chair Pro Tem Paloma Aguirre
  1) Direct the Chief Administrative Officer to implement an expanded enforcement strategy
  within the Office of Labor Standards and Enforcement that includes:
  a. Increased investigative capacity to address wage theft complaints, including
  proactive, industry-targeted investigations in sectors with high rates of violations;
  b. Enhanced enforcement of local and state labor standards; and
  c. Targeted outreach that connects workers directly to enforcement, including:
  i. Complaint intake and referral pathways that connect workers directly to the
  Wage Theft Enforcement Program and Workplace Justice Fund, through
  culturally competent, multilingual, and community-based outreach; and
  ii. Engagement strategies tailored to workers and industries at heightened
  risk of wage theft, including partnerships with trusted community-based
  organizations and worker-serving institutions that can identify violations and
  refer cases for investigation.
  2) Direct County Counsel, in coordination with the CAO and the Director of OLSE, to
  strengthen wage theft enforcement through enhanced legal coordination, including:
  a. Streamlining referral processes between OLSE and the Office of County Counsel;
  b. Expanding litigation pathways to pursue wage theft violations and recover unpaid
  wages; and
  c. Identifying and assigning appropriate legal resources to support a more proactive and
  effective enforcement strategy.
  3) Direct the CAO to evaluate opportunities to strengthen and expand the Wage Theft
  Enforcement Program and Workplace Justice Fund, including:
  a. Identifying sustainable funding sources, such as penalties, fees, settlements, grants,
  and other revenue streams associated with wage theft enforcement;
  b. Assessing strategies to increase access to these programs for workers with unpaid
  wage judgments;
  c. Evaluating strategies to improve the efficiency and timeliness of employer-side
  collection and cost-recovery efforts as enforcement capacity expands; and
  d. Identifying opportunities to align these programs with expanded enforcement efforts
  to maximize recovery and direct financial relief to impacted workers.
  4) Direct the CAO to report back to the Board within 120 days with a written update on
  implementation of this Board action, including progress on staffing, enforcement, wages
  recovered and judgments collected, Wage Theft Enforcement Program and Workplace
  Justice Fund improvements, and any additional resource or policy recommendations for
  Board consideration.
  5) Direct the CAO to express the County’s support for Assembly Bill 1838, consistent with
  Board Policy M-2.

  The proposed action supports the County of San Diego Strategic Initiative of Sustainability.

  Tijuana River Sewage Crisis (Districts: All)

  Recommendation by Chief Administrative Officer:
  Receive a presentation with the draft preliminary findings of the Economic Costs and Impacts of
  the Tijuana River Sewage Crisis study in response to the Board’s September 9, 2025 (17),
  direction.
  1)  ..End

  Equity Impact Statement
  The communities most directly affected by the Tijuana River sewage crisis include areas with
  socioeconomic and demographic characteristics that may increase vulnerability to economic and
  environmental disruptions. The draft study identifies a primary study area with approximately
  155,265 residents and 47,759 households. The study reports higher unemployment, a higher
  share of renters and cost-burdened renter households, lower educational attainment, and a higher
  share of households with incomes below $75,000 compared with the overall region. Presenting
  the draft findings supports a more complete understanding of how the crisis affects communities
  that have experienced prolonged exposure to pollution and related economic disruption.

  Sustainability Impact Statement
  Presentation of the draft findings supports the County of San Diego’s efforts to understand and
  address the long-term environmental, economic, and community impacts of the Tijuana River
  sewage crisis. The study provides information that can help guide investments and policy actions
  intended to improve environmental conditions, community well-being, economic resilience, and
  the long-term sustainability of affected communities.

  Fiscal Impact
  There is no fiscal impact associated with today’s presentation on the economic impacts of the
  Tijuana River sewage crisis. There will be no change in General Fund cost and no additional
  staff years.

  Business Impact Statement
  The draft study identifies significant pathways through which the sewage crisis has and may
  continue to affect businesses, including reduced beach visitation and tourism, lower customer
  activity, business disinvestment, and changes in business starts. Business survey respondents
  reported revenue impacts and indicated that continued conditions could result in reduced staffing,
  lost income, closure, or relocation. Draft recommendations include expanding
  economic-development and technical assistance for affected businesses, promoting destinations
  and activities that remain available during beach water closures, supporting events that increase
  foot traffic, connecting businesses with financial and marketing resources, and promoting South
  Bay assets and investment opportunities.

  Advisory Board Statement
  N/A

  Background
TUESDAY, SEPTEMBER 15, 2026  10
   The Tijuana River sewage crisis has affected communities and coastal areas in the South Bay for
  decades. Sewage and other pollutants carried through the Tijuana River watershed have
  contributed to prolonged beach water closures, degraded water and air quality, public health
  concerns, reduced recreational access, and economic disruption in affected communities.

  On September 9, 2025 (17), the San Diego County Board of Supervisors (Board) approved an
  item entitled, “Enhancing Regional Efforts and Federal Advocacy to Advance Solutions to the
  Tijuana River Sewage Crisis.” As part of that action, the Board directed the Chief Administrative
  Officer to fund and implement an Economic Impact Study assessing the full scope of losses
  caused by the sewage crisis, including impacts to small businesses, property values, and regional
  tourism, to strengthen future funding and mitigation efforts.

  The resulting Economic Costs and Impacts of the Tijuana River Sewage Crisis study is designed
  to identify and measure economic costs and impacts associated with the crisis and to provide
  evidence supporting a proactive approach to addressing those impacts. The draft methodology
  acknowledges that certain impacts can be monetized and directly attributed to the sewage crisis.
  It further recognizes that additional impacts can be quantified, though not reliably converted into
  monetary terms or conclusively linked to the crisis. Still others can be described or identified but
  cannot be appropriately quantified with the information currently available.

  The draft analysis identifies a series of negative economic impacts, including worsening water
  and air quality and prolonged beach water closures caused by increased sewage flows. These
  conditions have, in turn, contributed to reduced tourism and recreation, lost recreation value,
  costs to local businesses, property value declines, decreased transient occupancy tax revenues,
  increased public health and water treatment costs, population outmigration, and potential
  reductions in public school funding. The findings also identify potential impacts to public
  schools, with impacted districts experiencing larger reductions in enrollment and average daily
  attendance than other school districts in the region. Government expenditures associated with
  addressing the crisis are another component of the preliminary analysis. The study identifies
  approximately $1.3 billion in government spending to date based on various government reports,
  documents, websites, and news sources.

  Preliminary analysis indicates that the sewage crisis is causing substantial regional economic
  losses, with annual reductions in San Diego County’s economic output estimated between $125.6
  million and $503.5 million and discounted cumulative 20-year impacts ranging from $1.9 billion
  to $7.9 billion (in 2025 dollars). These estimates should be viewed as indicating the potential
  scale of economic effects, not as final damage determinations.

  Community and stakeholder engagement conducted for the study further illustrates these impacts
  on residents and businesses. This engagement took multiple forms, including virtual meetings
  with stakeholder discussion groups. These sessions gathered qualitative data such as anecdotes,
  stories, and lived experience. Invited stakeholders included municipal officials, environmental
  regulators, business leaders, chamber of commerce representatives, health experts, and
  community leaders. Additional community input was gathered via an online portal with four
  targeted surveys that were heavily promoted through multiple channels. Participants in the
  discussion groups and survey respondents reported reduced recreational activity, shorter or less
  frequent visits to impacted areas, concerns about health and quality-of-life, losses in business
  revenue, decreased staffing needs, and the potential for business closure or relocation if current

  The draft recommendations include providing consistent real-time communication to the affected
  communities across agencies and jurisdictions, providing support for affected businesses through
  promotional and technical assistance activities, strengthening regional and binational

  recommend support for the San Diego Regional Chamber of Commerce’s 5-Pillar Framework,
  predictable funding for operations and maintenance, preventive maintenance and monitoring, and
  a coordinated binational approach that moves the region from reactive repairs toward proactive
  system management.

  The findings and recommendations presented today remain preliminary until the final report by
